Given a contract created by another contract, is it possible to find the creator? If the answers are yes I think we can do without EVM versioning for some purposes. I don't *think* that information is stored anywhere. Some clients *may* have that information available, but I don't think it is anywhere in consensus in a way that is easily accessible. 1. Not in any easy way. For geth, you'd basically need to iterate through everything and trace 2. Same answer. (However, if you have a candidate, it's possible to verify that the candidate _is_ the creator) We've released Geth v1.10.1 with all agreed upon Berlin numbers baked in https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/releases/tag/v1.10.1 (and EIP2315 nuked out, as agreed) <@206016661470314496> 👍 had asked on a possible postponement of the Ropsten HF here https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/248#issuecomment-792573651 can you confirm that Ropsten can activate without problems with this release now? Ropsten is scheduled as previously That was the decision on ACD that it's better to keep the timeline, even at a sligt risk of Ropsten chaos I was afraid of that. It that means that we can't impose restrictions on EVM code and rather than versioning just say that everything placed on the chain by a transaction after some # must have met them. Or, if created by another contract, it's # ... In theory, we could introduce a hard fork that added a deploy time table. Can calculate it for all of history off-chain and agree on the tree root value for some historic block and then give nodes the ability to calculate forward from there. Then HF to introduce the root into consensus. This may not be any easier than just migrating all contracts to a new system in a 2 phase HF approach though. Not trying to promote this (it is discussed on <#706868829900505180>), but I think this explores some of these questions: https://notes.ethereum.org/@axic/evm-object-format I thought that one only discussed a new EVM architecture? Not how we could transition to jeVM versioning? Well the intro section collects some thoughts on what was tried so far. Including the validation ideas. It does not cover trying to figure out when something was created at 🙂 I feel like if we could solve EVM versioning we could solve a whole lot of problems at once. I think there are a lot of smart people involved in Ethereum development now who have learned from history and we could build a way better EVM now than we could 6 years ago. We just need a way to actually move to that new EVM. The main complaint against evm versioning is just introducing it for the sake of introducing (or some perceived flexibility) is not worth it if we need to keep the old EVM alive. So a lot of the changes we tried to do by either fitting into the current framework (even if it is suboptimal) or trying to deprecate things by not breaking anything in a major way. What I hope for is that with the new state expiry model there would be a very good disincentive to use old contracts ("epoch 0"), therefore adding evm versioning then means everyone would be incentivized to use that and to migrate to it. This EIP is proposed to be included in the London upgrade https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/260 Anyone know offhand why EIP-3 (`CALLDEPTH`) was withdrawn? I believe that the call depth limit was effectively (or maybe entirely) removed by the 63/64th gas rules that were added in one of the early forks. Also, I would imagine that it falls into similar categories to ORIGIN/GAS in that such an opcode would allow for a type of introspection into the execution environment that results in difficulties in maintaining backwards compatibility.

excerpts.author: gcolvin
excerpts.content:
Stupid questions --
1. Given a contract, is it possible to know the block number of the transaction that created it?
2. Given a contract created by another contract, is it possible to find the creator?

If the answers are yes I think we can do without EVM versioning for some purposes.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: I don't *think* that information is stored anywhere.  Some clients *may* have that information available, but I don't think it is anywhere in consensus in a way that is easily accessible.

excerpts.content:
1. Not in any easy way. For geth, you'd basically need to iterate through everything and trace
2. Same answer. (However, if you have a candidate, it's possible to verify that the candidate _is_ the creator)
